title: Zero Array Transformation I
statement:
`nums` is an array of integers, and each entry `queries[i] = [l_i, r_i]` of `queries` is an inclusive range of its indices. The queries are applied one after another in the given order. While applying query `i`, you choose any set of indices between `l_i` and `r_i` (the set may be empty) and subtract exactly `1` from the element at each chosen index.

Return `true` if the choices can be made so that every element of `nums` equals `0` after the last query, and `false` otherwise.
notes:
## Intuition

Each index can be handled on its own: a query that covers index `i` may lower `nums[i]` by one or leave it alone, whatever it does elsewhere. Nothing ever raises a value, so index `i` can reach `0` exactly when at least `nums[i]` queries cover it (use `nums[i]` of them and skip the rest). The question becomes: is every index covered at least as many times as its value?

Counting the coverage by walking every query's range costs O(n · q), up to 10^10 steps at these limits. A difference array records each range with two updates and recovers all the counts in one sweep.

## Approach

1. Make `diff` with `n + 1` zeros.
2. For each query `[left, right]`, add `1` at `diff[left]` and subtract `1` at `diff[right + 1]`, marking where the range starts and where it stops.
3. Sweep `i` from `0` to `n - 1`, adding `diff[i]` into the running total `cover`, which is then the number of queries covering index `i`.
4. If `cover < nums[i]`, too few queries reach index `i`, so return `false`.
5. If the sweep finishes, every index has enough coverage: return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 0, 1]`, `queries = [[0, 2]]`. The single query makes `diff = [1, 0, 0, -1]`. The sweep finds `cover = 1` at index 0 (needs 1), `1` at index 1 (needs 0) and `1` at index 2 (needs 1). No index falls short, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + q): two updates per query and one sweep over `nums`.
- Space: O(n) for `diff`.

## Pitfalls

- A query may skip an index, so extra coverage is harmless: test `cover < nums[i]`, not `cover !== nums[i]`.
- `diff` needs `n + 1` slots, because a range that ends at the last index writes to `diff[n]`.
- The order of the queries does not matter here; only how many of them cover each index.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `diff` | difference array: `+1` where a range starts, `-1` just past where it ends |
| `left`, `right` | the current query's range |
| `cover` | number of queries covering index `i` |
| `i` | the index being checked |

narration.3: A difference array with one spare slot, so a range ending at the last index still has somewhere to stop.
narration.4: Record every query's range; only how many queries cover each index matters, not their order.
narration.5: From index left onward, one more query covers each position...
narration.6: ...and from right + 1 onward this query no longer does.
narration.8: cover will count the queries that reach the current index.
narration.9: Sweep the indices from left to right.
narration.10: The running sum of diff is the number of queries covering index i.
narration.11: Fewer covering queries than nums[i] means this element can never reach zero.
narration.12: So the array cannot be turned into all zeros.
narration.15: Every index is covered at least nums[i] times, so the zero array is reachable.
